title: "The Memory Measurement Model (M3) with bmm"
subtitle: "Take-home notebook — Psychonomics 2026 bmm workshop, Part 2"
author: "Chenyu Li"

---

M3 is a computational measurement model of working memory (Oberauer &
Lewandowsky, 2019). It describes the processes that lead to correct responses
and to different types of errors. In M3, memory strength has two dimensions:
memory for the items themselves (**item memory**) and memory for their
relations to a context, such as a list position (**binding memory**). Every
response candidate receives activation that reflects the evidence for it in
working memory, and the candidates compete: the higher a candidate's
activation, the more likely it is selected. Correct responses and the
different errors draw on the two dimensions differently, so the frequencies of
the response categories let M3 estimate item memory and binding memory
separately.

This notebook uses a simple-span data set as its example and shows you how to
fit M3 to it with bmm: how to specify the model, check whether it reproduces
the responses, and interpret how both kinds of memory change as lists get
longer. The last section shows how to extend the model to complex span.

## Setup

Load the packages used in this notebook, and the colours and plot theme
shared by all workshop notebooks:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
options(width = 120)
library(bmm)
library(brms)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidybayes)
library(here)

source(here("_common.R"))  # shared workshop colors + ggplot theme
parameter_colors <- c(a = '#0028a5', c = '#dc6800', f = '#28a745')
source_colors <- c(Observed = '#008577', Predicted = '#8054a1')
source_shapes <- c(Observed = 16, Predicted = 17)
source_lines <- c(Observed = 'solid', Predicted = 'dashed')
```
:::


## Data

The workshop uses the open-set experiment (`openset`) from Oberauer (2019).
Twenty participants studied lists of words, each word in its own box, and were
then asked which word had been in one of the boxes. List words were drawn
without replacement from a pool of 1,198 nouns, so a word recurred only after
the whole pool had been used. Lists had 2, 4, 6, or 8 words. At test,
participants chose from a set of options that contained different numbers of
studied items and not-presented lures (NPL; words not in the list). Column
definitions are in the [codebook](../data/README.md).

Each row of the trial data is one test trial. It records the participant
(`id`), the set size, how many studied items (`rsizeList`, including the
correct one) and not-presented lures (`rsizeNPL`) were among the test
options, and the response category (`rcat`: 1 = correct, 2 = other studied
item, 3 = not-presented lure):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trials_simple <- read.csv(here("data", "m3_simple_trials.csv"))

head(trials_simple)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
          id setsize rsizeList rsizeNPL rcat
1 10_openset       2         1        1    1
2 10_openset       2         1        1    1
3 10_openset       2         1        1    1
4 10_openset       2         1        1    1
5 10_openset       2         1        1    1
6 10_openset       2         1        1    1
```


:::
:::


M3 analyzes the response frequency for each response category. Therefore, we
aggregate the trials into counts per category for each participant, set size,
and option combination. Because the probability of a category also depends on
how many options it had, we add one option-count column per category. Each
test has one correct option, so `n_corr` is 1. The other studied items are
the studied options without the correct one, so `n_other` is
`rsizeList - 1`. `rsizeNPL` counts the not-presented lures among the options,
so `n_npl` is `rsizeNPL`. Set size enters the model as a category, so we also
store it as a factor (`ss_fac`). Putting everything together, the data can be
summarized and phrased with the code:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat_simple <- trials_simple |>
  summarise(corr = sum(rcat == 1),
            other = sum(rcat == 2),
            npl = sum(rcat == 3),
            .by = c(id, setsize, rsizeList, rsizeNPL)) |>
  mutate(n_corr = 1L,
         n_other = rsizeList - 1,
         n_npl = rsizeNPL,
         ss_fac = factor(setsize))

head(dat_simple)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
          id setsize rsizeList rsizeNPL corr other npl n_corr n_other n_npl ss_fac
1 10_openset       2         1        1   23     0   0      1       0     1      2
2 10_openset       2         2        0   23     0   0      1       1     0      2
3 10_openset       2         2        2   23     0   0      1       1     2      2
4 10_openset       4         1        1   23     0   0      1       0     1      4
5 10_openset       4         2        0   23     0   0      1       1     0      4
6 10_openset       4         2        2   22     1   0      1       1     2      4
```


:::
:::


Each row contains the counts for one participant at one set size and one
combination of test options: 480 rows, 20 participants × 24 combinations.
The response-count columns sum to 23 in each row. A zero in an `n_*` column
means that category was absent from the options.

## Specify: model, formula, and priors

### Model

Every response option starts with the same baseline activation $b$. Studied
items receive additional activation from **item memory** ($a$). The correct
item receives further activation from **binding memory** ($c$), its
association with the probed position. The activation per option, $A$,
therefore differs between response categories:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(\mathrm{correct}) &= b + a + c \\
A(\mathrm{other}) &= b + a \\
A(\mathrm{NPL}) &= b
\end{aligned}
$$

To predict how often each category is chosen, M3 turns these activations into
category probabilities. With the softmax rule, a category's weight is its
number of options times the exponentiated activation per option. Dividing
each weight by the sum of all weights gives the probabilities:

$$
P(k) = \frac{n_k\exp(A_k)}{\sum_j n_j\exp(A_j)},
$$

where $A_k$ is the activation per option in category $k$ and $n_k$ is its
number of options. More options give a category more opportunities to be
selected, even when activation per option stays the same.

Adding the same $b$ to every option does not change the probabilities, so bmm
fixes $b$ at zero. The activations per option are then $a + c$ for the correct
item, $a$ for other studied items, and $0$ for lures.

The bmm function `m3()` specifies the model with four arguments:

- `resp_cats` lists the response-count columns.
- `num_options` lists the option-count columns, which must follow the same
  order as `resp_cats`.
- `version = "ss"` selects the simple-span activations above.
- `choice_rule = "softmax"` selects the softmax rule above.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
model_simple <- m3(
  resp_cats = c("corr", "other", "npl"),
  num_options = c("n_corr", "n_other", "n_npl"),
  version = "ss",
  choice_rule = "softmax"
)
```
:::


### Formula

In this data, participants' performance varied across set sizes, suggesting
that item memory and binding memory could change with set size. bmm can estimate
each parameter separately for each condition. We use `bmf()` to specify one
regression formula per parameter, starting with the parameter's name (`c ~`,
`a ~`). To get an estimate at each set size, the formulas use `ss_fac`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
formula_simple <- bmf(
  c ~ 0 + ss_fac + (0 + ss_fac | id),
  a ~ 0 + ss_fac + (0 + ss_fac | id)
)
```
:::


To make each coefficient the parameter's value at one set size, rather than a
difference from a reference set size, we remove the intercept with `0 +`.
We included random slope effect by adding `(0 + ss_fac | id)`, which lets each
participant deviate from these values at each set size and lets these
deviations correlate. The fit summary reports these coefficients:

| Coefficient | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `a_ss_fac2`, `a_ss_fac4`, `a_ss_fac6`, `a_ss_fac8` | Item memory $a$ at set sizes 2, 4, 6, and 8, respectively |
| `c_ss_fac2`, `c_ss_fac4`, `c_ss_fac6`, `c_ss_fac8` | Binding memory $c$ at set sizes 2, 4, 6, and 8, respectively |

### Priors

bmm estimates the model with Bayesian methods, so each parameter also needs a
prior. The coefficients of $a$ and $c$ are activations, so their priors
describe activation directly. We give each set-size coefficient a `normal(3, 1)` prior:
activations around 3 are most plausible, and about 95% of the prior lies
between 1 and 5. These priors apply to the set-size values, not to each
participant's activation. The participant-level standard deviations and
correlations keep bmm's default priors:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
priors_simple <- c(
  prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "a", coef = "ss_fac2"),
  prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "a", coef = "ss_fac4"),
  prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "a", coef = "ss_fac6"),
  prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "a", coef = "ss_fac8"),
  prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "c", coef = "ss_fac2"),
  prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "c", coef = "ss_fac4"),
  prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "c", coef = "ss_fac6"),
  prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "c", coef = "ss_fac8")
)
```
:::


## Fit: estimate the model and check the sampling

To estimate the parameters, we pass the formula, the model, the data, and the
priors to `bmm()`, which samples from the posterior with Stan:

- `formula`, `model`, `data`, and `prior` take the objects defined above.
- `file` saves the fitted model, and `file_refit = "on_change"` refits only
  when the model, data, or priors change.
- The other arguments control the sampling and are passed to `brms::brm()`;
  see its documentation for details.

Fitting would take a few minutes, so the workshop ships the fitted model in
`models/`. Because the saved fit matches this code, `bmm()` loads it instead of
fitting again:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_simple <- bmm(
  formula = formula_simple,
  model = model_simple,
  data = dat_simple,
  prior = priors_simple,
  file = here("models", "m3_simple"),
  file_refit = "on_change",
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  iter = 5000,
  warmup = 2000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  sample_prior = "yes",
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  seed = 2026
)
```
:::


To see the estimates, print the summary of the fit:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(fit_simple)
```

The summary has four parts:

- The **header** repeats the model, the links, the formulas, the data (480
  rows), and the sampling settings (12,000 draws after warmup).
- **Multilevel Hyperparameters** (`~id`) describe how much participants differ
  at each set size (`sd()`) and how their deviations correlate (`cor()`).
- **Regression Coefficients** are the set-size values of $c$ and $a$, the
  coefficients from the Specify section.
- **Constant Parameters** list the baseline $b$, fixed at 0.

In each row, `Estimate` is the posterior mean, `Est.Error` the posterior
standard deviation, and `l-95% CI` / `u-95% CI` the bounds of the 95%
credible interval. The last three columns are sampling diagnostics. Before
interpreting the estimates, check that the sampler worked:

- **`Rhat`** compares variation between and within chains. Values near 1
  indicate agreement; values above 1.01 warrant further investigation.
- **`Bulk_ESS` / `Tail_ESS`** describe how many independent draws the
  correlated MCMC draws are worth, for the bulk and tails of the posterior.
  They help assess the precision of posterior means and interval endpoints.
- **Divergent transitions** can indicate that the sampler has not explored
  the posterior reliably. They are a sampling problem, not a test of whether
  the model describes the observed responses.

To count divergent transitions, use `nuts_params()`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nuts <- nuts_params(fit_simple)

sum(nuts$Value[nuts$Parameter == "divergent__"])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0
```


:::
:::


With 5,000 iterations per chain (2,000 warmup), this fit has no divergent
transitions. Maximum Rhat is 1.00; minimum bulk and tail ESS are 1,512 and
3,156.

To confirm which priors the fit used, use `prior_info()`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior_info(fit_simple)
```

:::

The `user` rows (`ss_fac2` to `ss_fac8`) are the priors on the set-size values;
they override the general `bmm default` entries for $a$ and $c$. The other rows
are bmm defaults: the participant-level standard deviations (`sd`), their
correlations (`cor`), and the fixed baseline $b$. For a methods section,
`prior_info(fit_simple, format = "text")` writes the same information as
sentences.

### Optional: re-fit the model yourself

To fit the model yourself, change `file_refit = "on_change"` to `"always"` in
the code above. Re-fitting requires the Stan toolchain (`Install_Packages.R`,
Part 2).

## Evaluate: observed and predicted responses

Before interpreting the memory parameters, check whether the model describes
the responses, including both kinds of error. To compare the model with the
data, we compute the expected count in each response category with
`posterior_epred()`. It returns the expected count (trials × predicted
probability) for each posterior draw, data row, and category. `colMeans()` then
averages over the draws, which gives one expected count per row and category. We use 200
randomly chosen draws to keep this fast:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
expected_simple <- posterior_epred(fit_simple, ndraws = 200)

predicted_simple <- dat_simple |>
  select(id, setsize) |>
  bind_cols(as.data.frame(colMeans(expected_simple)))
```
:::


To prepare the data for plotting, we (1) stack the observed and predicted
counts, (2) sum each participant's counts over the option combinations and
divide by the total, and (3) average these proportions across participants and
compute their standard errors:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts_simple <- bind_rows(
  Observed = dat_simple |> select(id, setsize, corr, other, npl),
  Predicted = predicted_simple,
  .id = "source"
)

participant_props <- counts_simple |>
  summarise(across(c(corr, other, npl), sum),
            .by = c(source, id, setsize)) |>
  mutate(total = corr + other + npl) |>
  pivot_longer(c(corr, other, npl),
               names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(proportion = count / total)

pp_simple <- participant_props |>
  mutate(category = factor(category,
                           levels = c("corr", "other", "npl"),
                           labels = c("Correct", "Other studied items",
                                      "Not-presented lures"))) |>
  summarise(se = sd(proportion) / sqrt(n()),
            proportion = mean(proportion),
            .by = c(source, setsize, category))
```
:::


Plot the observed and predicted proportions by set size:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.25)

simple_predictive <- pp_simple |>
  ggplot(aes(x = setsize, y = proportion, group = source,
             color = source, shape = source, linetype = source)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = pmax(0, proportion - se),
                    ymax = pmin(1, proportion + se)),
                width = 0.12, position = dodge) +
  geom_line(position = dodge) +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = dodge) +
  facet_wrap(~category, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2, 4, 6, 8)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = source_colors) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = source_shapes) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = source_lines) +
  labs(x = "Set size", y = "Response proportion",
       color = NULL, shape = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_workshop() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

simple_predictive
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02_m3_files/figure-html/predictive-check-1.png){fig-alt='Observed and predicted open-set response proportions across three categories; the legend is on the right.' width=1152}
:::
:::


The model reproduces the observed proportions at every set size, for correct
responses and both kinds of error. We can therefore go on to interpret its
estimates of item memory and binding memory.

## Interpret: item memory and binding memory

To see how item and binding memory change with set size, summarise each
set-size coefficient by its posterior median and 95% credible interval:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
simple_parameters <- as.data.frame(fit_simple) |>
  select(starts_with("b_a_ss_fac"), starts_with("b_c_ss_fac")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = c("parameter", "setsize"),
               names_pattern = "b_(.)_ss_fac(.)",
               values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(setsize = as.integer(setsize)) |>
  summarise(median_qi(value), .by = c(parameter, setsize))

simple_parameters |>
  select(parameter, setsize, median = y, lower = ymin, upper = ymax) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

|a         |       4|   2.88|  1.86|  4.19|
|a         |       6|   2.68|  2.14|  3.45|
|a         |       8|   2.18|  1.79|  2.75|
|c         |       2|   4.92|  4.27|  5.72|

Plot the estimates by set size:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
simple_posterior <- simple_parameters |>
  ggplot(aes(x = setsize, y = y, color = parameter)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax)) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, nrow = 1,
             labeller = as_labeller(c(a = "Item memory (a)",
                                      c = "Binding memory (c)"))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2, 4, 6, 8)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 6), breaks = 0:6,
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = parameter_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Set size", y = "Activation") +
  theme_workshop()

simple_posterior
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02_m3_files/figure-html/posterior-plot-1.png){fig-alt='Item memory and binding memory medians and 95 percent credible intervals across set sizes, in blue and orange facets on a 0 to 6 scale.' width=1152}
:::
:::


Binding memory $c$ declines clearly as lists get longer, from 4.92 at set size
2 to 2.45 at set size 8. Item memory $a$ tends to decline as well, from 3.54 to
2.18, but its estimates are uncertain at small set sizes.
At set size 2, participants made only 6 errors, all to other studied items and
none to lures. Item memory $a$ is informed by how errors split between other
studied items and lures, so the data say little about $a$, and its estimate
stays close to the `normal(3, 1)` prior.

The posterior estimates allow us to test theoretical assumptions. For
instance, to examine whether item memory differs between set size 8 and set
size 2, we can use the `hypothesis()` function, which computes the difference
$a_8 - a_2$ in each posterior draw and tests whether it equals zero:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hypothesis(fit_simple, "a_ss_fac8 = a_ss_fac2")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

1 (a_ss_fac8)-(a_ss... = 0    -1.36      0.88    -3.14      0.3       0.52      0.34     
---
'CI': 90%-CI for one-sided and 95%-CI for two-sided hypotheses.
'*': For one-sided hypotheses, the posterior probability exceeds 95%;
for two-sided hypotheses, the value tested against lies outside the 95%-CI.
Posterior probabilities of point hypotheses assume equal prior probabilities.
```


:::
:::


How to read the output:

- **`Estimate`** is the posterior mean of $a_8 - a_2$. A negative value means
  lower item memory at set size 8.
- **`CI.Lower` / `CI.Upper`** bound the 95% credible interval of the
  difference.
- **`Evid.Ratio`** is the Bayes factor $BF_{01}$ for no difference
  ($a_8 = a_2$) against a difference: the posterior density of $a_8 - a_2$ at
  zero divided by its prior density at zero. Values below 1 favor a
  difference. It needs the prior draws saved by `sample_prior = "yes"`.
- **`Post.Prob`** is the posterior probability of no difference, assuming both
  hypotheses were equally probable beforehand.

Item memory is about 1.36 activation units lower at set size 8 than at set
size 2, but the 95% interval (−3.14 to 0.30) includes zero and
$BF_{01} = 0.52$, suggesting that the difference between set size 2 and set
size 8 was inconclusive.

## Extension: complex span

Li, Frischkorn, and Oberauer (2026), Experiment 1, added distractor processing
to the memory task. Participants viewed three target–distractor pairs, each
associated with a distinct context color, while judging which object was
larger in real life. In the **pre-cue** condition, the target in each pair
was designated before the size judgment. At test, a color cue indicated
which target to select from 12 image options.

Binding memory $c$ is again the association between an item and its context,
but here the context is the pair's color rather than the list position. A paired distractor shares the tested
target's color context; other distractors belong to the other pairs. The
workshop uses only the pre-cue condition: 45 participants, with one aggregated
row each. Exclusions and columns are documented in the
[codebook](../data/README.md).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat_complex <- read.csv(here("data", "m3_complex_span.csv"))

head(dat_complex, 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  participant condition corr other distc disto npl n_corr n_other n_distc n_disto n_npl
1           1       pre   31    17     4     6   1      1       2       1       2     6
2           2       pre   33    14     6     7   0      1       2       1       2     6
3           3       pre   42     7     3     4   4      1       2       1       2     6
```


:::
:::


### Specify

Distractors can also receive item and binding activation. M3 for complex span
therefore adds **filtering** ($f$), a multiplier on a distractor's item and
binding activation. With $f = 0$, distractors receive only the baseline
activation; with $f = 1$, they receive the same activation as targets. Lower
$f$ therefore means stronger filtering. The activation per option is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(\mathrm{correct}) &= b + a + c \\
A(\mathrm{paired\ distractor}) &= b + f a + f c \\
A(\mathrm{other\ targets}) &= b + a \\
A(\mathrm{other\ distractors}) &= b + f a \\
A(\mathrm{NPL}) &= b
\end{aligned}
$$

The `m3()` arguments work as described in [Model](#model). Here, `resp_cats`
and `num_options` list the five categories in the order of the equations
above, and `version = "cs"` selects these complex-span activations:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
model_complex <- m3(
  resp_cats = c("corr", "distc", "other", "disto", "npl"),
  num_options = c("n_corr", "n_distc", "n_other", "n_disto", "n_npl"),
  version = "cs",
  choice_rule = "softmax"
)
```
:::


The data contain a single condition, so each parameter gets one population
value and participant deviations from it:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
formula_complex <- bmf(
  c ~ 1 + (1 | participant),
  a ~ 1 + (1 | participant),
  f ~ 1 + (1 | participant)
)
```
:::


$a$ and $c$ get the same `normal(3, 1)` prior as in simple span (see
[Priors](#priors)). $f$ is estimated on the logit scale, where a
`logistic(0, 1)` prior makes every value of $f$ between 0 and 1 equally
plausible:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
priors_complex <- c(
  prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "a", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "c", coef = "Intercept"),
  prior(logistic(0, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "f", coef = "Intercept")
)
```
:::


### Fit

The fit uses the same settings and the same saved-fit handling as for simple
span (see [Fit](#fit-estimate-the-model-and-check-the-sampling)):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_complex <- bmm(
  formula = formula_complex,
  model = model_complex,
  data = dat_complex,
  prior = priors_complex,
  file = here("models", "m3_complex"),
  file_refit = "on_change",
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  iter = 5000,
  warmup = 2000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  sample_prior = "yes",
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  seed = 2026
)
```
:::

### Evaluate

To check whether the model describes all five categories, compute the expected
counts as for simple span (see
[Evaluate](#evaluate-observed-and-predicted-responses)):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
expected_complex <- posterior_epred(fit_complex, ndraws = 200)

predicted_complex <- dat_complex |>
  select(participant, condition) |>
  bind_cols(as.data.frame(colMeans(expected_complex)))
```
:::


Prepare the data for plotting in the same three steps. Each participant has
one row, so step 2 only divides the counts by their total:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts_complex <- bind_rows(
  Observed = dat_complex |>
    select(participant, condition, corr, distc, other, disto, npl),
  Predicted = predicted_complex,
  .id = "source"
)

participant_props_complex <- counts_complex |>
  mutate(total = corr + distc + other + disto + npl) |>
  pivot_longer(c(corr, distc, other, disto, npl),
               names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(proportion = count / total)

pp_complex <- participant_props_complex |>
  mutate(category = factor(category,
                           levels = c("corr", "distc", "other", "disto", "npl"),
                           labels = c("Correct", "Paired distractor",
                                      "Other targets", "Other distractors",
                                      "Not-presented lures"))) |>
  summarise(se = sd(proportion) / sqrt(n()),
            proportion = mean(proportion),
            .by = c(source, condition, category))
```
:::


Plot correct responses and errors in separate panels:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

complex_predictive <- pp_complex |>

  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = pmax(0, proportion - se),

                width = 0.10, position = dodge) +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = dodge) +
  facet_wrap(~response_type, nrow = 1, scales = "free", space = "free_x") +

  ggh4x::scale_y_facet(response_type == "Errors",

                              "Other targets" = "Other\ntargets",
                              "Other distractors" = "Other\ndistractors",
                              "Not-presented lures" = "Not-presented\nlures")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = source_colors) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = source_shapes) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Response proportion", color = NULL, shape = NULL) +

complex_predictive
```

### Interpret

$f$ is estimated on the logit scale, which keeps it between 0 and 1. Transform
its draws with `plogis()` before summarising; $a$ and $c$ stay on the
activation scale, as in simple span:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
complex_parameters <- as.data.frame(fit_complex) |>
  select(b_a_Intercept, b_c_Intercept, b_f_Intercept) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = "parameter",
               names_pattern = "b_(.)_Intercept",
               values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(value = if_else(parameter == "f", plogis(value), value)) |>
  summarise(median_qi(value), .by = parameter)

complex_parameters |>
  select(parameter, median = y, lower = ymin, upper = ymax) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|parameter | median| lower| upper|
|:---------|------:|-----:|-----:|
|a         |   3.10|  2.70|  3.56|
|c         |   2.12|  1.84|  2.41|
|f         |   0.66|  0.61|  0.70|


:::
:::


Plot the estimates, with $f$ in its own panel:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
complex_posterior <- complex_parameters |>
  mutate(scale = if_else(parameter == "f", "Filtering", "Activation")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = parameter, y = y, color = parameter)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax)) +
  facet_wrap(~scale, nrow = 1, scales = "free", space = "free_x") +
  ggh4x::scale_y_facet(scale == "Activation",
                       limits = c(0, 6), breaks = 0:6) +
  ggh4x::scale_y_facet(scale == "Filtering",
                       limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = parameter_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_workshop(base_size = 14)

complex_posterior
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02_m3_files/figure-html/complex-parameter-plot-1.png){fig-alt='Pre-cue parameter medians and 95 percent credible intervals: a and c on a 0 to 6 activation scale, f on a 0 to 1 filtering scale, in blue, orange, and green.' width=576}
:::
:::


Distractors keep about two thirds of a target's item and binding activation
($f$ = 0.66, 95% CI 0.61–0.70), so about a third of their activation is
filtered out. The posterior medians of item memory $a$ and binding memory $c$
are 3.10 and 2.12.
